title: Comprehensive Neuro Set 1: Brain Stem, Cerebellum, Basal Ganglia (Short Answer)

questions.prompt: What are the two major classifications of descending motor pathways based on whether they pass through the medullary pyramids?
questions.modelAnswer: Pyramidal tracts (corticospinal and corticobulbar) and extrapyramidal tracts (all others).

questions.prompt: Which specific descending tract is responsible for the execution of fine, discrete voluntary movements, particularly of the hands and fingers?
questions.modelAnswer: Corticospinal tract (specifically the lateral portion).

questions.prompt: Name the brain stem nucleus that gives rise to the rubrospinal tract and describe its primary effect on muscle groups.
questions.modelAnswer: The red nucleus; it produces excitation of flexors and inhibition of extensors.

questions.prompt: Contrast the effects of the pontine reticulospinal tract and the medullary reticulospinal tract on the activity of extensor muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: The pontine tract is generally excitatory to extensors; the medullary tract is generally inhibitory to extensors.

questions.prompt: Which extrapyramidal tract originates in the vestibular nuclei and causes powerful excitation of antigravity (extensor) muscles?
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral vestibulospinal tract.

questions.prompt: Explain the physiological basis of "decerebrate rigidity" in terms of excitatory and inhibitory brain stem influences.
questions.modelAnswer: It is caused by a lesion that removes inhibition from higher centers, leaving the powerful excitatory effects of the pontine reticular formation and lateral vestibular nucleus on extensor muscles unopposed.

questions.prompt: Identify the three functional divisions of the cerebellum and the specific aspect of movement each regulates.
questions.modelAnswer: Vestibulocerebellum (balance/eye movement); Spinocerebellum (synergy/coordination); Pontocerebellum (planning/initiation).

questions.prompt: List the three histological layers of the cerebellar cortex from innermost to outermost.
questions.modelAnswer: Granular layer (inner), Purkinje cell layer (middle), and molecular layer (outer).

questions.prompt: Name the only output cells of the cerebellar cortex and identify their primary inhibitory neurotransmitter.
questions.modelAnswer: Purkinje cells; they release GABA.

questions.prompt: Contrast "climbing fibers" and "mossy fibers" in terms of their origin and the type of electrical "spikes" they produce in Purkinje cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Climbing fibers originate in the inferior olive and produce complex spikes; mossy fibers originate in various brain stem/spinal centers and produce simple spikes (via granule cells).

questions.prompt: Define "synergy" within the context of cerebellar function.
questions.modelAnswer: The control of the rate, range, force, and direction of movement.

questions.prompt: List three classic clinical signs of a cerebellar lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: Ataxia (lack of coordination), dysmetria (overshooting/undershooting), and intention tremor.

questions.prompt: How does an "intention tremor" differ from a "resting tremor" in terms of the likely location of the neurological lesion?
questions.modelAnswer: Intention tremor suggests cerebellar disease; resting tremor suggests basal ganglia (substantia nigra) disease.

questions.prompt: Name the four primary nuclei that constitute the basal ganglia.
questions.modelAnswer: Striatum (caudate and putamen), globus pallidus, subthalamic nuclei, and substantia nigra.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental role of the basal ganglia in the planning and execution of movement?
questions.modelAnswer: To modulate thalamic outflow to the motor cortex to plan and execute smooth, coordinated movements.

questions.prompt: In the basal ganglia circuitry, which pathway (direct or indirect) is overall excitatory to the motor cortex?
questions.modelAnswer: The direct pathway.

questions.prompt: Describe the divergent effects of dopamine on the direct versus indirect pathways via its specific receptor subtypes (D1 and D2).
questions.modelAnswer: Dopamine excites the direct pathway (via D1 receptors) and inhibits the indirect pathway (via D2 receptors), meaning its overall effect is excitatory.

questions.prompt: What is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter used by the efferent neurons of the striatum?
questions.modelAnswer: GABA.

questions.prompt: Which specific nucleus of the basal ganglia is damaged in a patient presenting with wild, flinging movements known as hemiballismus?
questions.modelAnswer: Subthalamic nucleus.

questions.prompt: Explain the neurochemical and cellular defect responsible for Huntington's disease.
questions.modelAnswer: A hereditary disorder involving the destruction of striatal cholinergic and GABAergic neurons, leading to a release of inhibition.

questions.prompt: What is the primary pathological finding in Parkinson's disease?
questions.modelAnswer: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra.

questions.prompt: Why is L-dopa, rather than dopamine, used as a pharmacological treatment for Parkinson's disease?
questions.modelAnswer: Because L-dopa can cross the blood-brain barrier, whereas dopamine cannot.

questions.prompt: Define "dysdiadochokinesia" and identify the organ system involved.
questions.modelAnswer: The inability to perform rapid, alternating movements; it is associated with cerebellar lesions.

questions.prompt: Where are the "upper motoneurons" located, and what is their relationship to the "lower motoneurons" in the spinal cord?
questions.modelAnswer: Upper motoneurons are in the motor cortex (and brainstem centers); they synapse on and activate the lower motoneurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord.

questions.prompt: Define the "motor homunculus" and identify which body parts have the largest cortical representation.
questions.modelAnswer: A somatotopic map of the body on the motor cortex; the fingers, hands, and face have the largest representation due to their role in complex movements.
